job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Grace Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented room in a house in Eastfield with my friend Priya, and I have a desk by the window. Mornings are applications and a coding exercise, then I help at a weekly coding club for deaf teenagers, which is the best part of my week. Afternoons I go for a run and answer recruiter emails. My dad, who is a nurse, calls every evening to ask if there's news.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. Tell me about your degree and what you did for your internship.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied computer science at Harlow University, and my final project was a phone app that turns lecture speech into captions for deaf students, built with a group from the disability office. My internship was eight weeks on the data team of a health charity, cleaning donor records and building dashboards. Now I'm after a software job, ideally somewhere the work helps people directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief, honestly, because everyone's been shouting about this for years. In the group chat I'd say good, fewer surprises, now give me an interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my search is hard already without AI. There are plenty of openings near Eastfield but they want two years of experience for an entry-level post. I worry about that gap more than about any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with four applications a week and tailor each one. I'd finish a cloud certificate I've half done, because I'd rather show something than say it. I'd keep the coding club on Thursdays, since it keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy. My money's okay with some savings and my dad behind me, but every week without news wears on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said openings want two years of experience. What do you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I put the club and the captions app on my CV like a job, with numbers: twelve students, a term of weekly sessions. Recruiters seem to like numbers more than titles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you talk to when it gets heavy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, mostly, and my dad on the phone. He tells me it took him a year to find a proper ward job, which helps in a strange way.

say: I'd say it's a **relief**: fewer surprises, now someone please give me an interview.
I'd tell friends my real problem is the job market, not robots.
think: Openings want **two years** of experience for entry-level work, and that gap worries me more than AI.
Savings and my dad's backing keep me **steady**, but waiting still wears on me.
do: Finish the half-done **cloud certificate** before the new year.
feel: **Uneasy**: money's okay, but each week without news wears on me.
S0.quote: There are plenty of openings near Eastfield but they want two years of experience for an entry-level post.
fieldNote: Secure on money, yet the job-hunt gap between degree and **experience** is her real stress.
Turns **volunteer** work into numbers on her CV.
Draws comfort from her **father's** own slow job search.

steps.text: Send four tailored applications a week
Finish the cloud certificate by January
Keep running the Thursday coding club and list it as experience

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use this to make jobs better, not to cut them, and that governments should fund retraining. Online I'd probably post about how the captions app shows tech can help people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm anxious, because coding is on that list. Entry-level coding tasks, the bug fixes and small features I'd be given, are exactly what gets handed to AI first. Fewer junior posts, more people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI coding tools every week, properly, so I can say I work with them. I'd aim at jobs closer to people, like accessibility or health software, where someone has to talk to users. And I'd ask my charity contact whether the data team has any openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's something I can act on. I do worry about people who can't adapt as fast as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use AI tools weekly. How would that change your search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build one project where I used a coding assistant and wrote down what it got wrong. Employers want people who can check the machine, so I'd build a project that shows how I caught what the assistant got wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who worries you at your coding club?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older volunteers who've never used these tools. One of them, a retired teacher, says she's too old to learn. I'd sit with her and show her, because nobody else will.

say: I'd say we must use this to **improve** jobs, not cut them, and fund retraining.
Online I'd post about how my captions app shows tech **helping** people.
think: Entry-level coding like **bug fixes** and small features is what gets handed to AI first.
That means fewer **junior posts**, with more people like me chasing them.
do: Use **AI coding tools** weekly so I can say I work with them.
Target **accessibility** and health software, where users talk to you.
Ask my charity contact about openings on the **data team**.
feel: **Anxious**, but I can act on it, and I worry about people who adapt slower.
S1.quote: Employers want people who can check the machine, so I'd build a project that shows how I caught what the assistant got wrong.
fieldNote: Chooses **people-facing** niches because they're harder to automate.
Plans to show **evidence** of checking AI output, not just using it.
Concern for older **volunteers** shows her community streak.

steps.text: Build one project with an AI coding assistant and document its mistakes
Apply to accessibility and health software teams
Email the charity data team about openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd say that two years isn't something anyone can handle and the government has to step in now with serious income support. I'd probably join a demonstration, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel the floor go. Software is thinking work, so my whole degree gets cheaper than a subscription. The hands-on jobs hold a few years more, around 2031, but I don't have a hands-on skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd take whatever job I can get in the first six months, even if it's not great, just to have income on record. I'd move some savings into something safe and keep the rest. And I'd ask my dad about nursing assistant training, because care work needs people in the room for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can't see a plan that works, and my dad's wage can't carry both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Nursing assistant training is a big turn. Is that serious?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's half serious. I'd trial it with a short course, because I'm not sure I'm built for it. But my dad says the ward never has enough hands, and that matters now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guarantee income, pay for retraining without making you prove you're desperate first, and make employers report how many roles they replace. Honest numbers help.

say: Two years is **too fast**, and the government must step in with income support.
I'd join a **demonstration**, which I've never done.
think: Software is thinking work, so my degree feels like it loses its **value** overnight.
Hands-on jobs last until about **2031**, but I have no hands-on skill.
do: Take **any job** in six months to have income on record.
Move part of my savings somewhere **safe**.
Try a short **care assistant** course, since my dad says wards need hands.
feel: **Alarmed**: I can't see a plan, and my dad's wage can't carry us both.
S2.quote: Software is thinking work, so my whole degree gets cheaper than a subscription.
fieldNote: Alarm comes from the match **between** her skills and the card, not from panic.
Considers care work as a **robot-proof** fallback, though she is unsure of herself.
Wants **employers** to report how many roles they replace.

steps.text: Take the first reasonable job offered in six months
Move half of my savings into a safe account
Sign up for a short care assistant course
Join a demonstration for income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years I'd call a warning shot. I'd say to people that we should be building safety nets now, and I'd tell the coding club kids to learn how to think and not just how to code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me five years is workable. I can get a job, learn the tools, and have a few years behind me by 2031. But I'd be the junior person every employer thinks of when they cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job as soon as possible, then aim at jobs that ask me to explain things to users, like support engineering for accessibility software. I'd save half my pay and I'd start learning sign language properly, because it's useful and the kids love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit tired. There's room to move, but I can see the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sign language specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a thing I actually care about, and it makes me stand out for the jobs I want. A machine can caption speech, but it doesn't sit in the room and understand a teenager's day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your first employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honesty about whether my role is safe, and a training budget I can spend without asking twice.

say: Five years is a **warning shot**, so safety nets should start now.
I'd tell the club kids to learn how to **think**, not only how to code.
think: Five years is **workable**: a job, the tools and some experience before 2031.
Still, I'd be the **junior** every employer thinks of first when cutting.
do: Take a **first job** soon, then aim for user-facing accessibility support work.
Learn **sign language** properly, because it sets me apart.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit tired: there's room to move, but I can see the clock.
S3.quote: A machine can caption speech, but it doesn't sit in the room and understand a teenager's day.
fieldNote: Leans on a **human-contact** edge she actually cares about.
**Frames** her skills as caring plus tools, not tools alone.
Asks for honesty about job safety from a first **employer**.

steps.text: Take a first software job and ask about role security
Save half of every pay cheque
Take an evening sign language course this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years I'd say is a gift if people use it well, and a disaster if they don't. I'd tell friends to start retraining plans now and pester councillors about funding for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's quite manageable. By 2036 I could be a senior engineer or have moved into accessibility design. I'd worry about the people with no savings and no one behind them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a real career, learn the tools as they become normal, and maybe do a part-time master's in human-computer interaction. I'd also turn the coding club into a small charity with a proper budget, since that kind of work only grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It's the one I could plan around, and I like having something I want to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'using the decade well' look like for the country?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Free retraining, a wage floor for people whose jobs vanish, and schools that teach how to question what a machine tells you. None of that is impossible, it just needs someone to decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry the time makes people complacent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a lot. Ten years sounds like forever, so most people do nothing until year nine. That's what I'd push against.

say: Ten years is a **gift** if people use it well, and a disaster if they don't.
think: For me it's **manageable**: I could be senior or in accessibility design by 2036.
I worry about people with **no savings** and no one behind them.
do: Build a real **career** and pick up AI tools as they become normal.
Do a part-time **master's** in human-computer interaction.
Turn the coding club into a small **charity** with a budget.
feel: Fairly **calm**: this is one I could plan around.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like forever, so most people do nothing until year nine.
fieldNote: Time turns her anxiety into a **build-something** plan.
Worries about **complacency** at national level more than personal risk.
Social enterprise idea grows from her **volunteering**.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's in human-computer interaction
Register the coding club as a small charity
Push the council for retraining funds

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Probably the 2028 one, though it isn't the one that scares me most deeply. It's the one where nothing I plan survives, and my dad and I would have to rebuild from scratch. What helps is anything that gives people room to adjust: income support, retraining that actually works, and employers who tell you the truth early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how lonely it is to apply for jobs when everyone says the market is fine and you personally can't find one. I'd like someone to ask how that feels more often.

headlineQuote: Everyone says the market is fine and you personally can't find one.
portrait: Grace is a **23-year-old** computer science graduate sharing a rented room, still without an offer after several months of applying.
She is **progressive** and favours regulation and public support, and she runs a volunteer coding club for deaf teenagers.
She uses AI tools **now and then** and adopts them once they're proven, so she adjusts steadily rather than first.
Her mood rises with speed: **uneasy** in the mild picture, anxious in Steady Disruption, alarmed only in the 2028 world.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because nothing she plans would survive and her family would have to rebuild.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support**, retraining that works, and employers who say early when roles will shrink.
